deep.reconstruction:
Context (previous page): Hilbert characterises the Legendre polynomials P_n by a residue condition. Apart from log(x+1) and log(x-1), the integral ∫dx/((x^2-1)P^2) should contain no logarithmic terms. Equivalently, at every zero α of P the partial fractions of 1/((x^2-1)P^2) have only a double-pole term A/(x-α)^2 and no residue term a/(x-α). The P_n are then the denominators of the convergents of the continued fraction for ½log((x+1)/(x-1)). This page continues that line.

(a) Marginal note. He cites Heine, Kugelfunktionen I, pp. 137-138. Heine states that for the Lamé functions the integrals of the second kind likewise drop out, i.e. the analogous residue-free property holds.

(b) Programme of generalisations:
- apply the idea to algebraic functions such as sqrt(x) and to Riemann surfaces, i.e. to finding unbranched functions;
- ask for integrands whose partial fractions keep only the 1/(x-α)^3 terms and suppress the 1/(x-α)^2 terms as well (a higher-order analogue);
- note that the existence proof for automorphic functions leads to related questions, because a second-order linear ODE appears there;
- treat the Lamé equation the same way and see which continued-fraction expansion results. As transcribed the equation reads y'' = (ax+b)y, but that is the Airy-type equation; given the later mention of the elliptic surface and of ℘ on the next page, the Weierstrass form y'' = (a℘(u)+b)y is probably meant;
- ask what the quotient of two solutions of the Lamé equation maps onto. His guess is triangles on the elliptic Riemann surface.

(c) Worked example n=1 (my verification). P_1 = x and Q_1 = (x/2)log((1+x)/(1-x)) - 1, so y = -Q_1/P_1 = ½log((x-1)/(x+1)) + 1/x.
- Then y' = 1/(x^2-1) - 1/x^2 = 1/(x^2(x^2-1)), which is the integrand 1/((x^2-1)P_1^2).
- Replacing x by 1/x gives y = ½log((1-x)/(1+x)) + x, with y' = 1 - 1/(1-x^2) = -x^2/(1-x^2).
- Hence y = -x^3/3 - x^5/5 - ... near x=0. The inverse x(y) has a threefold branch point at y=0 (3 = 2n+1).
- y' ≠ 0 at every other finite x except ±1, where y has logarithmic singularities. So there are no other algebraic branch points.
- Exponentiating gives z = e^{2y} = ((1-x)/(1+x))e^{2x}. This is real for real x. For x = it both factors have modulus 1, so |z| = 1. These symmetries make the mapping easy to picture.

(d) Footnote (general n). Let y = ∫_∞^x dx/((x^2-1)P_n^2).
- At infinity the integrand is ~ x^{-2n-2}/c^2, so y ~ -x^{-(2n+1)}/((2n+1)c^2). Thus x = C·y^{-1/(2n+1)} + ..., a (2n+1)-fold branch point at y=0 (x=∞).
- dy/dx = 1/((x^2-1)P_n^2) never vanishes for finite x, so x(y) has no other algebraic branch points.
- At the zeros of P_n, y has a simple pole with no residue, so x is unbranched there.
- At x = ±1, y has logarithmic singularities, so x(y) never takes the values ±1.
- He claims these properties determine the integral.
- The Wronskian P_nQ_n' - P_n'Q_n = 1/(1-x^2) gives (Q_n/P_n)' = 1/((1-x^2)P_n^2). Since Q_n/P_n → 0 at ∞, y = -Q_n/P_n.
- y is a quotient of two solutions of Legendre's equation, so by Schwarz theory it maps a half-plane onto a (degenerate) circular-arc triangle. The angles are 0 at ±1 and (2n+1)π at ∞.
- Writing y = ½log((x-1)/(x+1)) - Z_n/P_n, the rational function Z_n/P_n is characterised by requiring that the derivative of ½log((x-1)/(x+1)) - Z_n/P_n never vanishes. That derivative equals [P^2 - (x^2-1)(Z'P - ZP')]/((x^2-1)P^2). The numerator must then be a nonzero constant, which is a Padé-type condition.
errors: As transcribed, the 'Lamé equation' y''=(ax+b)y is actually Airy's equation. The Lamé equation in Weierstrass form is y''=(a℘(u)+b)y, which is likely what is written or meant (the symbol may be ℘).

The footnote says x is 'nur für x=∞ verzweigt'. More precisely, the inverse function x(y) has its only algebraic branch point at y=0, the value corresponding to x=∞. The points y→∞ (at x=±1) are logarithmic, transcendental singularities. This is loose wording, not a mathematical error.
'(x-α)^2 übrig behalten' etc. are heuristic proposals, not derivations. The claim that the branching properties 'determine' the integral is asserted without proof but is plausible.
Sign conventions for Z_n are implicit. With Q_n = ½P_n log((x+1)/(x-1)) - W_{n-1}, one has Z_n = -W_{n-1}. This is consistent up to sign.

results.what: ∫_∞^x dx/((x^2-1)P_n^2) = -Q_n/P_n; Legendre polynomials characterised by the absence of residues at their zeros.
results.modern_name: Wronskian identity for Legendre functions / Christoffel–Heine formula; P_n as Padé denominators of log((x+1)/(x-1))
results.usually_credited_to: Heine, Christoffel (19th c.); continued fraction going back to Gauss

results.what: The inverse of y=∫dx/((x^2-1)P_n^2) has a single (2n+1)-fold algebraic branch point (at x=∞) and omits ±1. y maps a half-plane onto a circular-arc triangle with angles 0, 0, (2n+1)π.
results.modern_name: Schwarz triangle map for the Legendre equation (degenerate triangle)

results.what: n=1 explicit case: y=½log((1-x)/(1+x))+x has a triple branch point at 0. z=((1-x)/(1+x))e^{2x} is real on the real axis and unimodular on the imaginary axis.
Research programme: extend residue-free / Padé characterisation to Lamé equations, algebraic functions and Riemann surfaces, higher-order poles, automorphic functions and uniformisation.
results.modern_name: Padé approximation and orthogonal polynomials linked to Fuchsian ODEs; Heine–Stieltjes/Lamé polynomials; uniformisation

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics consists of known 19th-century facts (Heine/Christoffel, Schwarz maps). It is presented as a speculative research programme connecting continued fractions, residue-free integrals, Lamé equations and uniformisation. This is interesting as evidence of Hilbert's early interests, but contains no new theorem.
